content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"In a microservices architecture, data is distributed across multiple databases. Ensuring data consistency across these services without using traditional ACID transactions (like Two-Phase Commit, or 2PC) is a major system design challenge. The Saga pattern provides a sequence of local transactions that update data within individual services, eventually achieving eventual consistency."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"How the Saga Pattern Works"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Saga is a sequence of local transactions. Each local transaction updates database state within a single service. If a step fails, the saga executes a series of compensating transactions that undo the changes made by the preceding steps."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Local Transaction (T_i): A distinct unit of work performed by a single service."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Compensating Transaction (C_i): Actions that semantically undo the effects of local transaction T_i if the saga fails."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Orchestration vs. Choreography"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"There are two primary ways to implement the Saga pattern: Orchestration and Choreography."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Choreography: Services communicate via events without a central coordinator. Each service listens to events and decides the next action."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Orchestration: A central orchestrator (Saga manager) tells each service what local transaction to execute and manages the flow."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Example: Order Fulfillment Workflow"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider an e-commerce order system involving Order Service, Payment Service, and Inventory Service."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"1. Order Service creates Order (Status: Pending)\\n2. Payment Service processes payment\\n3. Inventory Service reserves items\\n4. If inventory fails -> Payment Service refunds payment -> Order Service marks Order Failed"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Design Considerations"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Lack of Isolation: Sagas lack ACID isolation. Intermediate states can be viewed by other concurrent transactions, requiring design patterns like Semantic Lock or Pessimistic Locking."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Idempotency: Because networks can fail and messages can be retried, all participating services must implement idempotent operations."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Saga pattern is an essential architectural pattern for managing distributed transactions in microservices. While it sacrifices immediate consistency for availability and scalability, proper handling of compensation logic and idempotency ensures robust fault-tolerant systems."}]
